description_full: StealthGas Inc., together with its subsidiaries, provides seaborne transportation services to liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) producers and users in Greece and internationally. The company's LPG carriers carry various petroleum gas products in liquefied form, including propane, butane, butadiene, isopropane, propylene, and vinyl chloride monomer, as well as ammonia. It also offers crude oil and natural gas. The company operates a fleet of 29 LPG carriers, including one JV vessel. StealthGas Inc. was incorporated in 2004 and is based in Athens, Greece.

financial_summary: StealthGas, Inc. is a micro-cap industrials business with a $297M market cap on $173M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $85M in free cash flow — roughly 49 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.40× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 25× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 36% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 32% operating margin runs 23pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 35% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 9% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 25% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 34% and a beta of 0.58, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $932K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash, 41% in the 2022 bear market and 83% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 70% below its DCF fair value of $26.64, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 12%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $21.73 to $33.37 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 5.0 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 1.7 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 3.5 vs 22.3 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-6%).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 28.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 45.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $14.00 on average, 77% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.00).
It converts 49% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.40x.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.0x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 17pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 2.9% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $99.1M (33% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.3% over 3 years, 3.6% over 5 years and 2.1% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 5.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 84.3% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.0x depreciation (0.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 50, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 35.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 39%.
